issues.legal_issue: A share company conducting banking business for members does not qualify for the mutuality principle where profits are distributed to shareholders as shareholders and the contributors to the fund are not identical with those entitled to participate in the surplus.
material_facts: The company conducted banking business restricted to its shareholders, accepting recurring deposits and advancing loans to members.
Interest earned on loans to members was the company’s main income.
After paying deposit interest and expenses, the company distributed the balance among members pro rata according to their shareholdings.
Shareholders entitled to participate in profits did not need to have made deposits or taken loans.
issues.conclusion: The mutuality principle did not exempt the company’s income. The company was assessable as a banking concern, and the answer to the referred question was affirmative.
issues.legal_principle: Under the principle in New York Life Assurance Co. v. Styles, mutuality requires that all contributors to the common fund be entitled to participate in the surplus and that all participators in the surplus be contributors; it is not enough that every member is entitled to contribute. A company may make profits from members as customers, and profits distributed to them as shareholders belong to them in that capacity, not as contributors. The Court applied Commissioner of Income Tax v. Royal Western Indian Turf Club Ltd., Municipal Mutual Insurance Ltd. v. Hills, and Thomas v. Richard Evans & Co.; it distinguished the principle applied to unincorporated associations in The National Association of Local Government Officers v. Watkins and rejected reliance on Board of Revenue v. Mylapore Hindu Permanent Fund Ltd. The company’s income remained business income assessable under section 10 of the Income-tax Act, 1922.

rule.if: mutuality_tax_case and incorporated_share_company and member_only_banking and main_income_from_member_loans and profits_distributed_by_shareholding and shareholders_need_not_contribute

predicates.mutuality_tax_case: The proceeding concerns whether a company’s income is exempt from tax on the ground of mutuality.
predicates.incorporated_share_company: The business is carried on through an incorporated company whose ownership is divided into shares.
predicates.member_only_banking: The company accepts deposits from and lends money to its members.
predicates.main_income_from_member_loans: The company earns most of its income from interest on loans to members.
predicates.profits_distributed_by_shareholding: The company distributes its surplus among members according to their shareholdings.
predicates.shareholders_need_not_contribute: Shareholders may receive a share of the surplus without having contributed to the fund through deposits or borrowing.

issues.definition: When an incorporated share company earns its main income from banking with members and distributes profits by shareholding to shareholders who need not contribute to the fund, mutuality does not exempt that income from tax.

issues.legal_issue: A High Court cannot order the refund of a reference fee as such, although it may assess costs so as to include the fee.
material_facts: The High Court ordered the refund of the assessee’s deposited reference fee as part of its costs order.
A subsidiary challenge was raised to the High Court’s jurisdiction to order that refund.
issues.conclusion: The High Court had no jurisdiction to order the refund of the reference fee as such, but it could, if it considered it appropriate, assess costs to include the amount deposited as the reference fee.
issues.legal_principle: The Court held that the High Court lacked jurisdiction to order the reference-fee refund, while recognizing that it could assess costs in a way that included the deposited fee. No provision or earlier case was cited for this ruling.

predicates.reference_fee_proceeding: The proceeding concerns an order made in connection with a fee deposited for a court reference.
predicates.high_court_ordered_fee_refund: The High Court directed that the deposited reference fee be refunded as such.

issues.definition: When a High Court orders a deposited reference fee refunded as such in a proceeding about that fee, the refund order is beyond its jurisdiction, though the fee may be included in an assessment of costs.
